title: Question 6

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text:
The paths of particles X and Z are shown.

Complete Fig. 6.1 to show possible paths for particles W and Y.

markscheme_points.text: W has deflection that is the mirror image of X
Y deflects downwards less than X or path of Y is parallel to particle Z

hints: Hint 1: Think about what force acts between the alpha particle and the gold nucleus, and in which direction it pushes the alpha particle.
Hint 2: Compare how close each particle comes to the nucleus - how does distance affect the size of the deflection for W compared to X, and for Y compared to X?
Hint 3: Look for symmetry above and below the nucleus, and remember that a far-away particle like Z is almost undeflected.
parts.proper_answer: W deflects upwards, away from the nucleus, with a path that is the mirror image of X. Y deflects downwards by a smaller angle than X, ending up approximately parallel to Z.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Repulsion Away From the Nucleus**
Both the alpha particle and the gold nucleus are positively charged, so they repel each other. The force is always directed away from the nucleus along the line joining them. That means a particle passing above the nucleus is pushed upwards, and one passing below is pushed downwards.

Step 2: **Using Symmetry for W**
W and X have the same starting distance from the central line. W is above, X is below, so they feel the same size of force but in opposite vertical directions. Therefore W must curve upwards in exactly the same way that X curves downwards - a mirror image.

Step 3: **Smaller Deflection for Y**
Y passes further from the nucleus than X does, so the electrostatic repulsion is weaker and acts for a shorter effective time. Y still deflects downwards, away from the nucleus, but through a much smaller angle than X. For a distant pass it leaves the region moving almost straight, nearly parallel to the undeflected particle Z.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Describe what may be inferred about the structure of an atom from the path of particle X.

markscheme_points.text: nucleus has most of the mass of the atom or nucleus is charged

hints: Hint 1: A light particle like an alpha can only bounce back through a large angle if it hits something much heavier and with a strong repulsive push.
parts.proper_answer: The large deflection of X shows the atom has a small, massive, positively charged nucleus.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Large Deflection Needs**
To turn a fast, massive alpha particle through a large angle you need a very strong repulsive force and a target much heavier than the alpha, otherwise the target would just recoil. This tells you all the positive charge and most of the mass of the atom is concentrated in a tiny nucleus.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text:
When a beam containing many alpha particles is incident on thin gold foil, nearly all of the alpha particles follow paths that are similar to the path of particle Z.

Describe what may be inferred from this about the structure of an atom.

markscheme_points.text: atom is mostly empty space or nucleus occupies a very small proportion of the space in the atom

hints: Hint 1: If almost every alpha goes straight through like Z, what does that say about how much of the atom is solid or blocks the path?
parts.proper_answer: The atom is mostly empty space, with the nucleus occupying only a very small fraction of the atomic volume.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why Most Pass Straight Through**
Particle Z is undeflected because it never comes close enough to feel a large repulsion. Since nearly all alphas behave like Z, most of them miss the nucleus completely. That is only possible if the nucleus is tiny compared to the atom, so the atom is mostly empty space.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: State the mass and the charge, in terms of the atomic mass unit $u$ and the elementary charge $e$, of an alpha particle.
hints: Hint 1: Recall what particles make up an alpha particle - it is the same as a helium-4 nucleus.
Hint 2: Count the total nucleon number for the mass in $u$, and the total proton charge for the charge in $e$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Structure of an Alpha**
An alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus, made of 2 protons plus 2 neutrons. Each nucleon has mass approximately $1\text{ u}$.

Step 2: **Mass and Charge**
Total mass is: $$m \approx 2(1\text{ u}) + 2(1\text{ u}) = 4\text{ u}$$ Only protons carry charge, each $+1e$, neutrons are neutral, so: $$q = +2e$$

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem: There are two types of hadron. The hadrons that are in alpha particles are each composed of three quarks.
parts.text: State the name of this type of hadron.
hints: Hint 1: Remember the two hadron families are distinguished by three quarks versus a quark-antiquark pair.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Three-Quark Hadrons**
Hadrons made of three quarks are called baryons. Protons and neutrons are the familiar examples, and they are exactly what is inside an alpha particle.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Show, by reference to their constituent quarks, that the hadrons in an alpha particle have charges of either zero or $+1e$.

markscheme_points.text: charge on up quark = (+)2/3(e) and charge on down quark = -1/3(e)
(proton is up up down and neutron is up down down) (2 x 2/3)e - (1 x 1/3) = 1e and (1 x 2/3)e - (2 x 1/3)e = 0

hints: Hint 1: Start by writing down the charge of an up quark and a down quark in units of $e$.
Hint 2: Add the three quark charges for a proton ($uud$) and for a neutron ($udd$) to show the totals are $+1e$ and zero.
parts.proper_answer: up quark charge $= +2/3e$, down quark charge $= -1/3e$. Proton ($uud$): $2(+2/3e) + (-1/3e) = +1e$. Neutron ($udd$): $(+2/3e) + 2(-1/3e) = 0$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Quark Charges**
Use the standard quark charges: $$q_{up} = +\frac{2}{3}e$$ $$q_{down} = -\frac{1}{3}e$$ An alpha contains only protons and neutrons, so you only need these two flavours.

Step 2: **Adding Charges**
A proton is $uud$: $$q_p = \frac{2}{3}e + \frac{2}{3}e - \frac{1}{3}e = +1e$$ A neutron is $udd$: $$q_n = \frac{2}{3}e - \frac{1}{3}e - \frac{1}{3}e = 0$$ This confirms the hadrons in an alpha have charges $+1e$ or zero.
